headings: What real-world value do syllogisms have?
Demonstrate how an informally articulated argument can be reformulated as a syllogism so the logic can be tested.
Explain the difference between validity and soundness.
Create a 10-item quiz on the entire thread above.
Provide 15 discussion questions relevant to the content above.
introHeading: Separate the inference from the truth of its premises
intro: Both original response tracks are retained, with corrected worked examples, two ten-item quizzes and two fifteen-question discussions. A valid argument preserves truth if its premises are true; a sound argument also has true premises.
description: Learn syllogistic structure, valid forms, common errors, and the distinction between deduction and uncertain inference.

replacements.1.1.0: A syllogism is an argument with two premises and a conclusion. In a standard categorical syllogism, three terms connect classes: the middle term appears in both premises and not in the conclusion. The major and minor terms are respectively the predicate and subject of the conclusion. Merely having this structure does not ensure validity.
replacements.1.1.3: Major premise: Contains the predicate term of the conclusion. It need not be universal simply because it is called major.
replacements.1.1.4: Minor premise: Contains the subject term of the conclusion. It need not describe a single individual.
replacements.1.1.5: Conclusion: The claim the premises are offered to support; whether it follows is what the validity test determines.
replacements.1.2.0: The examples below use two premises to support a conclusion. Some apply a general claim to an individual; that is a common use, not the definition of every categorical syllogism.
replacements.1.2.1: Major premise: In categorical form, the premise containing the conclusion’s predicate term.
replacements.1.2.2: Minor premise: In categorical form, the premise containing the conclusion’s subject term.
replacements.1.2.12: A valid inference can contain a false premise. It then lacks soundness, even if the conclusion happens to be true. For example:
replacements.1.2.13: Major premise: All birds can fly. This universal statement is false; exceptions defeat “all.”
replacements.1.2.15: Conclusion: Therefore, Tweety can fly. The inference is valid, but the argument is unsound because its major premise is false. The premises do not establish whether this particular bird can actually fly.
replacements.1.2.16: Validity concerns what follows under the premises. Soundness requires that those premises also be true. A false premise does not force a false conclusion.
replacements.2.1.2: Situation: A simplified hypothetical legal rule can illustrate applying a rule to a case. The example is not a statement of any jurisdiction’s actual penalty law.
replacements.2.1.3: Assumed rule: Every person convicted under the specified rule must pay the stated penalty.
replacements.2.1.4: Case premise: The defendant was convicted under that rule.
replacements.2.1.6: Value: The conclusion follows if the rule and case premise apply. The syllogism exposes what must be checked; it does not establish the actual law, facts, or fairness of the outcome.
replacements.2.1.8: Situation: A symptom pattern can prompt investigation, but reasoning from symptoms to a disease is usually uncertain inference rather than a conclusive categorical syllogism.
replacements.2.1.9: Proposed premise: A specified symptom pattern is compatible with tuberculosis. Compatibility is weaker than diagnosis or even a demonstrated high probability.
replacements.2.1.10: Case premise: The hypothetical patient has that pattern.
replacements.2.1.11: Limited conclusion: Tuberculosis is one possibility under the proposed premise. This does not establish that the patient has it.
replacements.2.1.12: Value: Formalization reveals the limited conclusion and missing diagnostic evidence. It does not ensure correct treatment; CDC diagnostic guidance describes evaluation beyond a symptom list.
replacements.2.1.15: Major premise: Every product whose relevant revenue exceeds its total relevant costs is profitable over the specified period.
replacements.2.1.16: Minor premise: Product X meets that revenue-and-cost condition for the period.
replacements.2.1.18: Value: The conclusion follows from the stated accounting condition. The original combination of high satisfaction and low production costs was insufficient: it omitted revenue, volume, and other costs.
replacements.2.1.19: These examples make assumptions inspectable. A valid form cannot turn an uncertain medical inference, an unverified legal rule, or incomplete business data into an established fact.
replacements.2.2.2: Proposed premise: Peanut allergy can cause an adverse reaction after exposure. “Can” does not mean that everyone has the same reaction or that every reaction has this cause.
replacements.2.2.4: Tentative interpretation: Allergy is a possibility, but no deductively certain diagnosis follows from the stated conditional and symptoms.
replacements.2.2.5: The example illustrates inference to a possible cause. A causal condition cannot simply be reversed, and further clinical assessment matters; see the NIAID-sponsored diagnostic guidelines.
replacements.2.2.8: Analysis: Improvement after taking something does not establish that it caused recovery; even an established effect in one case would not guarantee it in every other case.
replacements.2.2.9: What a reconstruction exposes: To infer a guaranteed result, the speaker would need a universal effectiveness premise and evidence that this case satisfies its conditions. Neither is supplied. Do not invent a medicine’s antiviral effect to repair the argument.
replacements.2.2.12: Proposed premise: Every planet with a strong magnetic field has a liquid metal core. This is an oversimplified scientific premise, not an established general rule.
replacements.2.2.14: Conclusion under that premise: Jupiter has a liquid metal core. The form would be valid, but the premise is not warranted as stated. NASA describes a dynamo associated with liquid metallic hydrogen; a strong field alone does not establish a conventional molten-metal core.
replacements.2.2.15: Formalizing a scientific argument helps identify the model or empirical generalization that needs testing. Logical form alone does not validate that model.
replacements.3.1.4: Conditional premise: If the specified emissions trajectory continues, warming will continue to increase. This retains the intended conditional instead of claiming that every individual action failing to reduce emissions causes warming.
replacements.3.1.5: Case premise: Continuing the specified practices maintains that trajectory.
replacements.3.1.6: Conclusion: Under these premises, continuing those practices means warming will continue to increase.
replacements.3.1.7: Logic test: This is modus ponens after the trajectory connection is made explicit. Its empirical premises need separate support. The policy claim “we must cut emissions” also needs an explicit goal or normative premise; it is not supplied by the prediction alone.
replacements.3.1.14: Logic test: Invalid: from adequate funding → better outcomes and not adequate funding, not better outcomes does not follow. That denies the antecedent. A counterexample could be an underfunded school with better outcomes for another reason. The original report of poor performance is a separate observation, not a deduction from lack of funding.
replacements.3.1.19: Required case premise: John lacks access to the relevant care. The informal argument supplies only lack of insurance; the reconstruction therefore needs an additional connection rather than silently substituting access for insurance.
replacements.3.1.21: Logic test: The displayed no-access inference is valid under its premises. Its universal premise and John’s actual access require evidence. The informal argument’s insurance-to-access step remains unestablished.
replacements.3.2.2: Implicit premise: If my visit will be cold throughout and my activities do not require shorts, I will not need to pack shorts. The original response accidentally wrote “require wearing shorts,” reversing the intended support.
replacements.3.2.3: Case premise: The visit will meet those conditions. “Seattle is always cold” is an unsupported blanket assertion, not a verified forecast for this trip.
replacements.3.2.4: Conclusion: Therefore, under those premises, I will not need shorts. The inference works; the weather and activity premises still need checking.
replacements.3.2.7: Major premise: Every restaurant causally responsible for one food-poisoning case is a bad place to eat. This sweeping evaluative premise is open to challenge.
replacements.3.2.8: Minor premise: The restaurant caused the friend’s illness. Becoming ill after a visit does not, by itself, establish this causal premise.
replacements.3.2.9: Conclusion: The restaurant is a bad place to eat. It follows if the stated premises are true, but neither causal attribution nor the sweeping evaluation is established merely by the anecdote.
replacements.3.2.12: Implicit decision rule: I will not undertake any activity I find boring. This makes the practical conclusion explicit without replacing “I will not do it” with “it is a waste of time.”
replacements.3.2.13: Case premise: I find studying for this test boring.
replacements.3.2.14: Conclusion: I will not study for the test. The inference follows from that decision rule; the rule’s wisdom is a different question.
replacements.4.1.18: Soundness: Unsound because “all fruits are animals” is false. The altered example avoids ambiguity between culinary and botanical uses of “vegetable.”
replacements.4.1.20: No such example exists under the standard definition. Soundness includes validity, so “invalid but sound” is contradictory, not merely difficult to illustrate.
replacements.4.1.26: Validity: The conclusion introduces mammals without a linking premise. A model with a sparrow that is both bird and fish but not mammal satisfies the premises and falsifies the conclusion. That countermodel establishes invalidity.
replacements.4.1.28: Validity rules out true premises with a false conclusion. Soundness adds actual truth of the premises. Neither consistency alone nor a true conclusion establishes validity.
replacements.4.2.6: This form is valid. It is sound if Whiskers really is a cat, together with the true classification premise. A fictional name in an example does not independently establish a real-world case premise.
replacements.4.2.10: Invalid but Sound: Impossible under the definition
replacements.4.2.13: Example: Everyone who eats chocolate has a cavity; I have a cavity; therefore I ate chocolate. This deliberately reverses the implication to supply an invalid form.
replacements.4.2.14: The revised example affirms the consequent: a cavity could occur without eating chocolate, even under the stated premise. The universal premise is also unwarranted. The original “ate chocolate, therefore will get a cavity” form would be valid if the times matched; a false causal premise would make it unsound, not invalid.
replacements.5.1.9: In a categorical syllogism, which conclusion term occurs in the minor premise?
replacements.5.1.13: A two-premise argument. In categorical form, the middle term links the premises and does not occur in the conclusion; the conclusion relates the other two terms.
replacements.5.1.20: The subject term of the conclusion; the minor premise need not be a claim about one individual.
replacements.5.1.21: The shared term “animals” does not force an overlap between dogs and cats. The premises can be true with disjoint dog and cat classes; the traditional diagnosis is an undistributed middle, not the absence of a middle term.
replacements.5.2.2: Which premise in a categorical syllogism contains the conclusion’s predicate term?
replacements.5.2.5: What unsupported inferences occur in “This medicine cured my cold, so it will definitely cure yours too”?
replacements.5.2.6: Expose the conflict in this argument: “It always rains in London, so I won’t need to pack an umbrella.” What explicit bridge premise would support the stated conclusion?
replacements.5.2.9: Classify this argument’s validity separately from the truth of its first premise: “Anyone who studies hard gets good grades. I studied hard, so I got good grades.”
replacements.5.2.10: Which argument is valid and has true premises under the stipulated case fact that Fido is a dog? a) All dogs are mammals; Fido is a dog; therefore Fido is a mammal. b) Most fast-food eaters gain weight; I ate fast food yesterday; therefore I gained weight. c) Everyone who speeds gets a ticket; I did not get a ticket; therefore I did not speed.
replacements.5.2.16: First, recovery after treatment does not alone establish causation. Second, a single outcome does not establish a universal guarantee for another person.
replacements.5.2.17: A bridge such as “For every trip with constant rain, I need no umbrella” would yield the stated conclusion with the trip premise, but is not justified here. The more ordinary umbrella-needed bridge yields the opposite conclusion. The constant-rain claim also needs evidence; do not silently reverse the conclusion to conceal the conflict.
replacements.5.2.20: Valid by modus ponens. The universal premise may be false because other factors affect grades; that challenges soundness, not the conditional inference.
replacements.5.2.21: a), given the stipulated Fido fact. Option c is also valid by modus tollens, but its universal ticket premise is false as a real-world guarantee. Option b draws a necessary individual conclusion from “most,” so it is invalid.
replacements.6.1.5: Can an invalid syllogism have true premises and a false conclusion? Why can a valid one not do so?
replacements.6.2.15: What checks would be needed before relying on a language model’s classification of an argument as valid or sound?
